{{Short description|On when a function on convex body K does not decrease if K is translated inwards}}
{{about|Anderson's theorem in mathematics|the Anderson orthogonality theorem in physics|Anderson orthogonality theorem|the superconductivity theorem|Anderson's theorem (superconductivity)}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Anderson's theorem''' is a result in [[real analysis]] and [[geometry]] which says that the [[integral]] of an integrable, symmetric, unimodal, non-negative function ''f'' over an ''n''-dimensional [[convex body]] ''K'' does not decrease if ''K'' is translated inwards towards the origin. This is a natural statement, since the [[graph of a function|graph]] of ''f'' can be thought of as a hill with a single peak over the origin; however, for ''n'' ≥ 2, the proof is not entirely obvious, as there may be points ''x'' of the body ''K'' where the value ''f''(''x'') is larger than at the corresponding translate of ''x''.

Anderson's theorem, named after [[Theodore Wilbur Anderson]], also has an interesting application to [[probability theory]].

==Statement of the theorem==
Let ''K'' be a convex body in ''n''-[[dimension]]al [[Euclidean space]] '''R'''{{sup|''n''}} that is [[symmetry|symmetric]] with respect to reflection in the origin, i.e. ''K''&nbsp;=&nbsp;&minus;''K''. Let ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''{{sup|''n''}} → '''R''' be a non-[[negative number|negative]], symmetric, globally integrable function; i.e.
* ''f''(''x'') ≥ 0 for all ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''{{sup|''n''}};
* ''f''(''x'') = ''f''(&minus;''x'') for all ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>;
* <math>\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}} f(x) \, \mathrm{d} x < + \infty.</math>

Suppose also that the super-[[level set]]s ''L''(''f'',&nbsp;''t'') of ''f'', defined by

:<math>L(f, t) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^{n} | f(x) \geq t \},</math>

are [[convex set|convex subsets]] of '''R'''<sup>''n''</sup> for every ''t''&nbsp;≥&nbsp;0. (This property is sometimes referred to as being '''unimodal'''.) Then, for any 0&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''c''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;1 and ''y''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>,

:<math>\int_{K} f(x + c y) \, \mathrm{d} x \geq \int_{K} f(x + y) \, \mathrm{d} x.</math>

==Application to probability theory==
Given a [[probability space]] (Ω, Σ, Pr), suppose that ''X''&nbsp;:&nbsp;Ω&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''{{sup|''n''}} is an '''R'''{{sup|''n''}}-valued [[random variable]] with [[probability density function]] ''f''&nbsp;:&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>&nbsp;→&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;+∞) and that ''Y''&nbsp;:&nbsp;Ω&nbsp;→&nbsp;'''R'''{{sup|''n''}} is an [[Statistical independence|independent]] random variable. The probability density functions of many well-known probability distributions are ''p''-[[concave function|concave]] for some ''p'', and hence unimodal. If they are also symmetric (e.g. the [[Laplace distribution|Laplace]] and [[normal distribution]]s), then Anderson's theorem applies, in which case

:<math>\Pr ( X \in K ) \geq \Pr ( X + Y \in K )</math>

for any origin-symmetric convex body ''K''&nbsp;⊆&nbsp;'''R'''<sup>''n''</sup>.
